synthesis.headline: Enhanced severe risk in Oklahoma and Kansas tonight as western trough ejects and Plains cyclone deepens
synthesis.narrative:
The western trough behind four days of Southwest flash flooding is now lifting out, and tonight brings the second and stronger night of Plains severe weather. SPC has an Enhanced risk (level 3 of 5) over north-central Oklahoma and south-central Kansas. Warm-sector supercells should form there by 22-23Z, and the tornado threat peaks as low-level shear strengthens around 00Z. Dryline storms from western Kansas to southwest Texas should merge into a squall line (QLCS) by evening, bringing damaging winds and tornadoes overnight, possibly into western Missouri. North Texas gets late-afternoon storms with hail early, then mainly damaging gusts. At the surface the low is still a loose cluster of 999-1004 mb centers from the Dakotas to Oklahoma, and WPC expects it to deepen quickly across the northern Plains. Ahead of the cold front, 60s dewpoints contrast with 30s-40s air behind it. WPC has a Slight flash-flood risk over eastern Oklahoma and western Arkansas. Elsewhere, onshore flow around a 1032 mb high moving off the East Coast keeps heavy rain on Florida's southeast coast (also Slight), while the Northeast stays dry and mild.

At 500 mb a high-amplitude, positively tilted trough covers the West and central US, with its base near the Four Corners. A 70-85+ kt jet core runs over the Southwest and northern Mexico and curves northeast through the central Plains. A closed low near 560 dam over the Dakotas and Minnesota sits on the trough's northern flank, still part of the larger circulation rather than a detached cutoff. Downstream, heights of 580-590 dam from the Mississippi Valley to the Southeast mark the ridge that is pulling Gulf moisture north. Satellite imagery shows a dry intrusion wrapping around the trough's southwest side, sharpest over eastern Colorado. The flow is progressive, so the system keeps moving east. SPC's main uncertainty is slow early storm organization because low-level winds have weakened.

On Tuesday the trough swings toward the Mississippi Valley as the surface low stalls over southern Minnesota. SPC has a Marginal risk from east Texas and central Louisiana to southwest Illinois, with isolated damaging gusts or a brief tornado; widespread cloud and weak lapse rates limit it. Heavy rain concentrates near the Arkansas-Tennessee-Mississippi border (Slight). From Thursday into the weekend the front reaches the East Coast, bringing widespread showers and storms, followed by cooler, drier air. A low northeast of the Bahamas could keep rain going along the coast. The ejection does not end the western trough pattern. CPC charts deepen a Gulf of Alaska trough for November 7-11 and extend it down the coast to California by November 9-15, while ridging moves north toward the Arctic and into the East. Expect Pacific systems into the Northwest and broad warmth across the northern tier.
synthesis.climate_context: A strong El Niño is underway and still strengthening. The Oceanic Niño Index reached +2.16 C for July-September, up from -0.39 C last winter, with each season warmer than the last. That fits an active southern-stream jet like the one now over the Southwest and northern Mexico, which fed the recent desert flooding. Early November is a secondary severe-weather season for the southern Plains and Mississippi Valley. The hurricane season has four weeks left but no active storms. The Atlantic has only a 20 percent chance of a possibly subtropical low within seven days. A system east-southeast of Hawaii is far from North America. Teleconnection indices are a month out of date, so they are not used here.
synthesis.regional_notes: No SPC mesoscale discussions are active. Last night's Texas Panhandle discussion (MD 2428) ran out at 11Z as storms there weakened, and no watch was issued. Expect watches across Kansas and Oklahoma this afternoon. On Florida's southeast coast, onshore-flow rain could cause localized flooding today and Tuesday. A 953 mb low over the Bering Sea is packing tight isobars toward the Alaska-Yukon edge, and a 998 mb low lies off the Pacific Northwest coast. Southern Canada has only a weak pressure gradient, and a frontal wave is crossing the Maritimes.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary:
This 0900Z Monday 2 November analysis is dominated by a broad, multi-centered low complex over the central Plains, with labeled centers near 1001, 999, 1002 and 1004 mb clustered from the Dakotas down through Nebraska, Kansas and Oklahoma. These look like a family of weak, similar-strength lows sharing one large cyclonic circulation, so no single center clearly dominates. A cold front trails south-southwestward from this complex through the southern Plains toward west Texas, with a stationary or warm boundary marked in the Dakotas/Minnesota region. Another cold front arcs across the Great Basin and Southwest toward southern California, near a 1012 mb low.

The highs are modest. Weak centers of roughly 1024-1026 mb sit over the Pacific Northwest and the northern Rockies/northern Plains, and a high near the Mid-Atlantic coast is the main feature east of the Appalachians. None of these is strong enough to be the story on its own. A frontal system with a trailing cold front and a wave also sweeps across the Canadian Maritimes and northern New England at the top right.

The pressure gradient looks tightest around the central Plains lows, where closely spaced isobars wrap the cluster, and across the northern Rockies and Great Basin between the Northwest high and the interior troughing. Gradients are much slacker across the Southeast, the Gulf Coast and the Ohio Valley, where isobars are sparse and winds are light.

For moisture and lift, the cold front through the southern Plains is the obvious focus. It has a clear thermal contrast, with 60s to near 70F dewpoint-region temperatures ahead of it over Texas and the lower Mississippi Valley versus 30s to 40s behind it. Warm-sector air streaming north from the Gulf toward the Plains lows implies low-level moisture transport into the frontal zone, though the chart alone cannot show the depth of that moisture or the upper support. The Great Basin front looks drier, with cool 30s to 40s readings and little warm-sector moisture evident.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary:
This CMC surface analysis, valid 00Z Monday 2 November 2026, is drawn on a polar projection, so the pole and Arctic Ocean sit near the top-center and the North American continent fills the lower half. The dominant feature is a very deep low, labeled 953 mb, in the far left of the frame, apparently over the northern Pacific or Bering Sea sector, with a tightly packed set of concentric isobars and a looping occluded front wrapped around it. A long cold front trails from that system southeastward across the Pacific toward the western North American coast, where a weaker low near 998 mb sits just offshore of the Pacific Northwest and another low near 1000 mb lies farther south off the coast.

Over the continental interior the pattern is far less energetic. A cluster of weak lows between 1001 and 1004 mb sits over the central United States, with a front and warm-sector boundary extending northeast from the northern Plains low, while broad high pressure of 1021 mb over the northern Rockies and Prairies side and 1032 mb over the eastern United States dominates the south and east. The cross-border gradient looks modest, with no tight isobar packing evident over the southern Canadian provinces, though the chart is dense enough that fine detail there is hard to read.

In the Arctic, a strong 1037 mb high sits near the center-right of the polar region with a ridge of 1041 mb farther to the right over what appears to be the Siberian side. A deep low near 962 mb with an occluded structure lies on the right side of the chart over the northern Eurasian or Barents-Kara sector. Several weaker lows between 979 and 994 mb line the central Arctic and the area near the Canadian Archipelago and Greenland, and the exact placement of these relative to specific islands is uncertain at this scale. The strongest pressure gradients over land are at the left edge, where the 953 mb low's packed isobars approach the Alaska-Yukon side, but the chart does not make clear how far inland that gradient extends.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary:
The 500 mb pattern at 1200 UTC 2 November 2026 shows a high-amplitude, positively tilted trough over the western and central U.S. Its base is plotted near the Four Corners to southern Rockies, and the downstream ridge axis lies over the Mississippi Valley into the Great Lakes, with heights running roughly 580-590 dam across the Midwest, Ohio Valley and Southeast. A smaller cutoff-like feature appears over the northern Plains near the Dakotas/Minnesota (red L), with a closed contour near 560 dam, which is embedded in the broader cyclonic flow and appears to lie on the northern flank of the trough rather than at its base. Whether that low is fully detached from the westerlies is not clear from the contours alone, and the nearby heights are low enough (roughly 560-570 dam) that it reads as part of the larger trough circulation rather than a distinct, self-retaining cutoff.

The jet is the shaded wind field. A strong, broad maximum with winds exceeding 70-85 kt (dark red core) sits over the Southwest and northern Mexico/southern Rockies at the trough base, with the stronger flow curving northeastward through the central Plains toward the Great Lakes on the eastern side of the trough. This implies a southwesterly jet corridor on the downstream side, consistent with strong height gradient along the 570-580 dam contours. Farther north, a second jet streak (red/orange, 60-80+ kt) appears off the Canadian Maritimes and northeast Atlantic, and weaker green-shaded flow lies over the Pacific Northwest.

The trough axis tilts positively (southwest-northeast), and the flow looks progressive rather than blocked, with no evident high poleward of the low to form a Rex or omega configuration. The geometry instead is a strongly amplified western trough with a downstream ridge over the eastern third of the country, a pattern that favors poleward heat and moisture transport ahead of the system and cold advection behind it. Temperatures at 500 mb (dashed blue) are coldest, roughly -18 to -24 C, in the northern trough and near the Dakotas low, moderating to about -5 to -10 C across the Southeast.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary:
A broad, elongated swath of orange-to-red dry air stretches from the northern Rockies and High Plains (Wyoming, Colorado, western Nebraska) southwest across New Mexico and Arizona into northwestern Mexico. It lies on the western and southwestern flank of the large comma-shaped cloud mass over the upper Midwest and northern Plains, so it sits on the cyclonic side of the flow, consistent with a dry intrusion wrapping around the trough. Its sharpest and most saturated portion, over eastern Colorado and the central High Plains, is the best candidate for a stratospheric-intrusion signature. The imagery shows dryness only, so descent is implied rather than shown.

The dense white cloud shield over Minnesota, Wisconsin and the upper Great Lakes marks the cold-topped core of the system, with a trailing band of thinner cloud streaking south-southwestward through the Mississippi Valley into Louisiana and the northwestern Gulf. Cold blue-purple tones over the Pacific Northwest and the far western edge of the domain, together with the cloud near the left margin, suggest a second, upstream trough approaching, though the limb distortion there limits interpretation.

A second sharp boundary runs from the southeast U.S. coast near the Georgia-Carolina border southwest across Florida and the eastern Gulf. Dry orange air lies on its west side and moist green and cloudy air on its east side. This transition is the likely jet corridor in the eastern half of the domain, again an inference from the airmass contrast rather than a plotted axis. Along and east of it, organized cloud bands stretch from the Carolinas offshore, with bright, deep convective clusters over south Florida and the adjacent waters. Another large area of convective cloud covers the western Atlantic and Caribbean, east of the Bahamas and over Hispaniola and Puerto Rico, within the moist tropical air. The Gulf of Mexico, Mexico and the southeastern U.S. are mostly green, indicating moist air aloft with little deep convection.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary:
This GOES-19 Air Mass RGB from 13:20Z on 2 November 2026 shows a sharp contrast between a broad green tropical airmass over the low latitudes and purple-blue, cold dry upper-tropospheric air across Canada and the Arctic rim. The color boundary between them, running from the northern Plains and Great Lakes region northeastward toward Newfoundland and the western North Atlantic, marks the airmass gradient and implies the polar jet corridor. A bright white cloud shield over the northern Plains and upper Midwest, with an adjacent orange-red dry slot to its southwest, points to a deep upper trough and cyclone there, with comma-shaped cloud wrapping into the Great Lakes. The orange-red patch west of the cloud shield is the compact, cyclonic-side feature that fits a dry-air or stratospheric intrusion signature, though the chart shows only the color, not potential vorticity.

In the Atlantic, an arc of cloud and a narrow bright band curve along the northeast limb near the edge of the disk, consistent with a frontal cloud band, though the strong limb distortion makes its exact position uncertain. East of Florida and the Bahamas, scattered white clusters stretch east-northeast along the boundary toward the central Atlantic, a trailing frontal and upper-level cloud zone. A larger cluster of white cloud near the right edge of the disk, at roughly 10-20N, lies far enough east that its placement relative to the African coast cannot be judged from this view.

Across the tropics, a band of broken convective cloud runs west to east across the eastern Pacific south of Mexico and Central America, then connects to deeper clusters over Panama, Costa Rica, and the southwestern Caribbean, with more convection near northern Colombia and Venezuela. This reads as an active ITCZ and monsoon-trough zone rather than a single organized system; no closed circulation or tropical cyclone is evident at this resolution. The broad olive-orange areas in the subtropics on both sides of the equatorial cloud band, over the northeast Pacific off Mexico and the southeast Pacific, indicate drier mid- and upper-level air, consistent with subsidence under subtropical ridging rather than stratospheric intrusion.

In the Southern Hemisphere, a large white cloud mass over southeastern Brazil and the adjacent western South Atlantic, with a comma-like tail extending east, suggests a frontal system and convection near the coast. Further south, several swirls and orange-red features around the southern South Atlantic and southeast Pacific mark midlatitude lows, one near the lower right edge of the disk showing a tight red-orange core with a dry-slot appearance.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary:
This CPC outlook for November 7-11, 2026 favors above-normal temperatures across most of the contiguous US, with no below-normal category plotted anywhere in the lower 48. Probabilities peak at 80-90% over the northern High Plains, centered on the Montana-North Dakota-South Dakota area, and remain in the 60-80% range across the northern Rockies, Upper Midwest and much of the Plains. Confidence steps down in a smooth gradient toward the southeast: 50-60% across California, the Great Basin, the Southwest and the central Plains, then 33-50% (leaning above) through the Ohio Valley, mid-Atlantic and southern Plains into central Texas. A broad near-normal (equal chances) zone covers the Gulf Coast, Southeast and most of Texas. New England and the Northeast are favored above at roughly 50-70%, and Maine reaches the 60-70% shading.

The strongest signal sits in the northern tier with the weakest in the Southeast, so the favored warmth is concentrated poleward of a southwest-to-northeast gradient. The chart plots only probabilities of tercile categories, so the implied pattern is an inference rather than a plotted field. A warm anomaly this large and this far north is consistent with a ridge or a flat, Pacific-dominated flow suppressing Arctic air intrusions over the northern US, while the neutral Southeast fits a weaker signal south of the main flow. Such a setup would favor persistence of the current regime into the 6-10 day window rather than a breakdown, since the outlook shows no cold signal anywhere in the lower 48.

In Alaska, the east and interior lean above normal (up to 50-60%), while western and southwestern Alaska are near normal and the Aleutians are marked below normal. Hawaii is favored above normal at roughly 40-60%. Note that these are probabilities of category, not magnitudes, so 80-90% does not mean an extreme departure, only high confidence in the upper tercile.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is the CPC 6-10 day 500 mb heights and anomalies prognostic, made 01 Nov 2026 and valid Nov 7-11. One reading note: the contours are labeled in meters (5160 to 5820 m, i.e. 516-582 dam), and the dashed anomaly lines are also in meters at 60 m intervals, so the red labels of 30, 90, 150 are positive departures of roughly 3, 9 and 15 dam, not extraordinary values.

The dominant feature is a large, deep negative anomaly over the eastern North Pacific and Gulf of Alaska, with blue dashed contours (down to the -150 and -210 m range, about -15 to -21 dam) covering a broad area off the British Columbia and Alaska coasts. This pairs with a closed 5220 m low on the northwestern edge of that trough. The trough axis appears to run roughly along or just west of the Pacific coast, tilting toward the Gulf of Alaska.

Downstream, strong positive anomalies cover western and central Canada and the northern Plains. The red contours peak near 150 m (about 15 dam) over the Canadian Prairies and Hudson Bay region, with positive anomalies stretching southeast across the Great Lakes toward the Northeast. The ridge axis, read from the northward bulge of the height contours, runs from the Intermountain West and northern Rockies northeastward through central Canada toward Baffin Island and the Arctic, where a separate +90 m center sits over northern Greenland and the Arctic Ocean side.

The zero-anomaly line (purple dashed) cuts through the western US, so positive anomalies reach into the Pacific Northwest, Rockies and northern Great Basin while the Southwest and Pacific coastal margin lie near or below zero. A second broad negative center sits over the North Atlantic east of Newfoundland, completing a trough-ridge-trough pattern across the continent.

On amplification, the pattern reads as a strongly meridional, high-amplitude wave with the ridge displaced poleward and eastward over Canada rather than anchored over the West Coast. Positive anomalies over western North America appear to be retreating northeast in longitude relative to the coast, with the Pacific trough taking over the coastal region. The tightly packed contours south of the ridge imply a strong westerly flow corridor across the northern tier of the Lower 48, but the flow overall is not becoming more zonal in this view.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is the CPC 8-14 day 500 mb heights and anomalies prognostic, made 01 Nov 2026 and valid Nov 9-15. Solid green contours are mean heights, labeled in meters (5160 to 5820, i.e. roughly 516-582 dam) with the stated 60 m interval, and the dashed lines are anomalies. Their labels read as 30, 90, 150 and 210, which matches height anomalies in meters, so the largest values are on the order of 20 dam, not 200. The sign convention is red positive and blue negative.

A positive anomaly is clearly present over northern Canada, the Arctic Archipelago and Greenland, with red centers near the 90 label northwest of Hudson Bay and over the high Arctic. A second red area covers the eastern half of the continent from the Great Lakes through eastern Canada. Positive anomalies are not evident over western Canada, the northern Rockies or the northern Plains. That region sits under blue dashed contours, so the ridge has not set up there.

The dominant negative anomaly is a broad blue area from the Gulf of Alaska and the Pacific Northwest south across California and the Great Basin, with the deepest labeled values (210, 150) over the northeast Pacific off British Columbia and Washington. The mean contours bulge southward there, consistent with a deep trough along or just off the West Coast, with a ridge axis implied downstream over the Arctic and the eastern continent. Another blue anomaly appears over the North Atlantic east of Newfoundland.

Taken together, the pattern is a Pacific trough with high-latitude and eastern ridging, and the ridge core sits well north, not retreating toward the Southwest or northern Mexico. The Southwest and northern Mexico show only weak anomaly contours (zero-line purple dashes), so there is no strong ridge there.

sources.title: Excessive Rainfall Outlook (Day 1)
sources.summary:
Only two of the four categories appear on this Day 1 outlook, valid 12Z Monday November 2 to 12Z Tuesday November 3, 2026. A broad green Marginal (at least 5%) area stretches from the central and northern Plains southward through the Mississippi Valley to Texas. It runs from the Dakotas and Minnesota, including the western Great Lakes edge near Lake Superior, down through eastern Nebraska and Iowa, western Missouri and Arkansas, then southwestward across eastern Oklahoma into central and northeast Texas. A second, much smaller Marginal area hugs the Florida east coast and peninsula.

The highest category anywhere on the chart is Slight (at least 15%), drawn in yellow with an orange outline in two places. The larger Slight area sits over eastern Oklahoma and adjacent western Arkansas, embedded within the Marginal corridor. The other is a narrow sliver along the Florida east coast, roughly from the central peninsula southward. No Moderate or High risk is drawn.

The elongated, southwest-to-northeast orientation of the Plains and Mississippi Valley area is consistent with rainfall organized along a front or a slow-moving trough axis rather than terrain, though the chart plots only risk categories and does not show the front itself. The Florida area is narrow and coast-parallel, which fits a different regime, likely onshore flow along the coast, and nothing on the chart points to a tropical system.

sources.title: Excessive Rainfall Outlook (Day 2)
sources.summary: This Day 2 Excessive Rainfall Outlook, valid 12Z Tuesday Nov 3 to 12Z Wednesday Nov 4, 2026, shows two categories: a broad Marginal (green, at least 5%) area and a small embedded Slight (orange outline, yellow fill, at least 15%) area. No Moderate or High risk is drawn. The Marginal area forms a long, north-south corridor running from the upper Gulf Coast of Louisiana and the Texas-Louisiana border region northward through Arkansas and the Mississippi Valley, reaching into southern Missouri and the Ohio Valley vicinity near the Illinois and Indiana border. The Slight area sits within that corridor over the lower Mississippi Valley, roughly spanning the Arkansas-Tennessee-Mississippi border region west of the Tennessee River valley. A second, much smaller Marginal area hugs the Florida peninsula's east coast. Because the shape is elongated along a southwest-to-northeast axis and bounded sharply on both sides, it appears consistent with a slow-moving frontal boundary or training convection along a corridor, though the chart itself shows only risk categories and not the underlying system. I cannot tell from this chart alone how the risk compares with what a Day 1 outlook showed, so I won't claim it has grown or relaxed.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary:
WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion, issued 257 AM EST Monday, November 2, 2026, valid 12Z Monday November 2 through 12Z Wednesday November 4.

A lee-side cyclone in the Central High Plains, ahead of a deep Western U.S. upper trough, is forecast to deepen quickly while crossing the Northern Plains, bringing increasing winds, showers, and thunderstorms. A cold front emerging this afternoon should bring a round of severe thunderstorms and isolated to scattered flash flooding to the Central and Southern Plains. The heavy rainfall focus then shifts east toward the Mississippi Valley and Upper Midwest ahead of the front, with severe weather also possible across the Lower and Mid-Mississippi Valley.

Separately, onshore flow around a large high pressure system sliding off the East Coast will keep heavy rain going over the southern Florida Peninsula today. The same high will maintain dry, mild weather across much of the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary:
SPC Day 1 outlook, issued 0658 AM CST Nov 2, 2026, valid through 12Z Nov 3. Enhanced risk (level 3 of 5) for north-central Oklahoma and south-central Kansas. Damaging winds and a few tornadoes are expected across the southern and central Plains this afternoon into tonight.

A deep Four Corners shortwave trough and a lead trough drive surface lows and a cold front across the Plains, with 60s dewpoints and strong southwesterly flow aloft.

Greatest tornado risk is north-central OK into south-central KS, with warm-sector supercells expected by 22-23Z and strengthening low-level shear around 00Z. Dryline storms from western KS to southwest TX merge into a QLCS by evening, bringing damaging winds and tornadoes overnight, possibly into western MO. North TX sees late-afternoon storms, mainly damaging gusts and early large hail, with some embedded tornadoes. Florida Peninsula: scattered showers and storms, with no tornado probabilities.

Uncertainty: early storm organization may be slow due to weakened low-level flow.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary:
SPC Mesoscale Discussion 2428, issued 0301 AM CST Monday, November 2, 2026 (valid 0901-1100Z), covers parts of the Texas Panhandle. The severe threat is waning as thunderstorms become elevated and displaced behind a surface cold pool, and overall convective intensity has decreased over the past hour per MRMS echo tops and GOES IR imagery. Lingering MUCAPE of about 1000-1500 J/kg and strong deep-layer shear remain, but robust surface-based convection is quickly diminishing.

A few shallow towers along the New Mexico/Texas state line west of Lubbock could intensify as they move east, according to the 06Z HRRR. Forecasters consider this unlikely to pose a substantial severe threat through early morning, given weak radar and satellite presentation and lingering inhibition downstream.

Probability of watch issuance is 5 percent; no watch is expected. Stated maximum probable hazards: tornado up to 90 mph, wind gusts up to 60 mph, and hail up to 1.25 inches.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
**Atlantic (as of 700 AM EST Mon Nov 2 2026):** Low pressure is likely to form along a weakening frontal boundary a few hundred miles northeast of the Bahamas within a couple of days. It may acquire some subtropical characteristics late this week while drifting over the western Atlantic, but development chances end by the weekend as it moves east or northeast into unfavorable conditions. Formation chance: near 0 percent through 48 hours, 20 percent through 7 days.

**East Pacific (as of 400 AM PST Mon Nov 2 2026):** A broad low well east-southeast of Hawaii is producing disorganized showers and thunderstorms. Conditions appear generally favorable for gradual development, and a tropical depression is likely to form during the middle to latter part of this week as it moves west to west-northwest at 10 to 15 mph over the Central Pacific. Formation chance: 20 percent through 48 hours, high at 70 percent through 7 days.

sources.title: NHC Active Storm Advisories
sources.summary: NHC currently lists no active tropical cyclones, and no advisories are being issued. The product contains no named systems, positions, intensities, forecast tracks, or watches and warnings to report. No as-of date was included with this product, so the currency of this status cannot be confirmed from the material provided.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary:
ENSO state, Oceanic Niño Index: El Niño conditions are present and strengthening. The latest season shown, JAS 2026, has an ONI of +2.16 C, well above the +0.5 C El Niño threshold and in strong-event territory.

The index has risen steadily through the table. It moved from -0.39 C in DJF 2026 (a cold-leaning, La Niña-side value) to +0.11 C in FMA, then +0.46 C in MAM, +0.95 C in AMJ, +1.39 C in MJJ, +1.80 C in JJA, and +2.16 C in JAS. Each successive season has been warmer than the last, and the rate of increase has been accelerating through mid-2026.

The table does not state an as-of date, so the timing of the most recent observations relative to today cannot be confirmed from this product.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary:
STALE DATA: The CPC teleconnection indices below are dated 2026-09-30, 33 days before this product's reporting, and CPC has not updated them. Do not treat them as current. They are observed values, not forecasts, and summer teleconnections are weak, so use them only as directional context.

PNA: +0.12 on 2026-09-30. The 7-day mean is -0.41, up from -1.51 the prior week, so the index has been rising toward neutral-to-positive after a negative stretch.

AO: -0.26 on 2026-09-30. The 7-day mean is +0.04, down from +1.73, so the index has been falling and recently turned negative.

NAO: -0.78 on 2026-09-30. The 7-day mean is -0.15, down from +0.28, so the index has been falling, with its latest value the most negative in the 14-day window.
